description: We built Rotawise, an open source crop rotation advisor for Nigerian smallholder farmers. It reads NASA HLS imagery to recover each plot's season history since 2020, scores soil fatigue with SoilGrids soil data, tests rotations against NASA POWER climate records and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections for the 2040s, prices fertilizer savings in naira and delivers advice in Hausa or English on any phone via USSD. Live at https://rotawise-five.vercel.app
summary: Rotawise gives every smallholder farm in Nigeria a memory. It reads every NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel 2 image of a plot since 2020 and rebuilds how the field has been used season by season, showing when it carried cereals, when it carried legumes and when it lay bare, with a confidence score for each reading. It combines that field memory with NASA POWER climate records, NASA NEX GDDP CMIP6 climate projections and SoilGrids soil data to compare at least three rotation strategies, including the one the farmer already uses. For each option it explains why it was suggested, the evidence behind it, the fertilizer savings in naira, its effect on Striga weed, its fit with future rainfall and heat, and what a local extension agent should check. Farmers receive the advice in Hausa or English on any phone through USSD, and extension officers plan for whole communities on a web dashboard. Rotawise supports farmer judgment rather than replacing it.
details: Many farmers in northern and central Nigeria plant maize on the same land season after season because they have no plot specific evidence that changing crops pays. Field trials in the northern Guinea savanna show maize yields rising by around 68 percent after soybean and 49 percent after cowpea, soybean supplying up to 55 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare, and two years of legumes cutting Striga infestation by 76 percent. Rotawise turns that science into a decision a farmer can act on. We built five pilot farms in Zaria, Dawakin Tofa, Bida, Bokkos and Gwagwalada. Each pilot point is a real cropland block, chosen automatically from the ESA WorldCover 10 metre land cover map near each local government area. For each farm the engine works in four steps. First, it builds a field memory: for every growing season it takes the cloud masked NDVI time series from NASA HLS, measures the dry season baseline, the peak, the green up date and the length of the green period, and classifies the season as cereal like, legume or short cycle, or bare, with a confidence score. It never claims to name a specific crop, because 30 metre pixels on small intercropped plots cannot do that reliably, and it asks the farmer to confirm. Second, it scores soil fatigue from 0 to 100 using the run of consecutive cereal seasons, a robust Theil Sen trend in peak greenness, and SoilGrids organic carbon, nitrogen and pH, and it lists each driver. Third, it summarizes the plot's climate from NASA POWER daily data: typical season rainfall, rain onset, the longest dry spell and days above 35 degrees Celsius. A built in quality check leaves out any season whose rainfall is more than twice or under 40 percent of the median, because these are data errors in the source product, and the dashboard says which years were left out. It then applies the change in season rainfall and hot days that two NEX GDDP CMIP6 models project for the 2040s. Fourth, it compares the farmer's current rotation with maize then soybean, maize then cowpea, maize then groundnut and sorghum then cowpea. Each option shows its nitrogen credit for the plot's agro ecological zone, urea bags saved, fertilizer saved and extra maize in naira at prices the user can edit, Striga reduction, water fit now and in the 2040s, the information gaps, and the risks for local review. We ran the full pipeline on real NASA data for all five farms: 1,824 cloud free HLS readings, ten seasons of NASA POWER weather and CMIP6 projections for each farm. Four of the five farms show cereal planted season after season, with soil fatigue scores between 52 and 60, and the Bida farm scores 53 from low soil nitrogen and carbon. Rotawise recommends maize then soybean for the four Guinea savanna farms and sorghum then cowpea for Dawakin Tofa in the drier Sudan savanna, where today's rainfall meets less than half of what maize needs and the crop faces more hot days. On the Zaria farm, switching to maize then soybean saves 0.6 to 2.4 bags of urea per hectare, worth about 30,000 to 120,000 naira at 50,000 naira a bag. Rotawise is built with Python for the data pipeline, a FastAPI service with rate limiting, caching, health checks and metrics, a MapLibre web dashboard, and a stateless USSD handler in the Africa's Talking format. Every agronomic coefficient lives in one file next to its published source, and the project ships with a privacy policy and automated tests. It is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Source code: https://github.com/Jothankato05/Rotawise Our next step is to measure the season classifier against labelled fields and pilot Rotawise with extension services and cooperatives in the five LGAs. Because Rotawise reads plot history from orbit instead of asking for it, it can scale to any plot in West Africa that NASA satellites observe, and reach farmers who have no smartphone or internet. NASA data used: We use NASA Harmonized Landsat Sentinel 2 (HLSL30 and HLSS30 version 2.0), accessed through Microsoft Planetary Computer, to build the plot level season history from Fmask cloud masked NDVI. We use the NASA POWER daily agroclimatology API (bias corrected precipitation and maximum temperature) to compute season rainfall, rain onset dates, the longest dry spell and days above 35 degrees Celsius. We use NASA NEX GDDP CMIP6 daily projections from the ACCESS CM2 and MRI ESM2 0 models, accessed through the NASA Center for Climate Simulation THREDDS server, to compare May to October rainfall and hot days in the 1995 to 2014 baseline with the 2040s under SSP2 4.5 and SSP5 8.5. The dashboard can display NASA GIBS MODIS Terra true colour imagery as a base layer. Other data and references: HLS includes European Space Agency Sentinel 2 observations, harmonized by NASA. We use the ESA WorldCover 10 metre land cover map (CC BY 4.0), accessed through Microsoft Planetary Computer, to place every pilot point on confirmed cropland. Soil properties come from ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 (CC BY 4.0). Agronomic coefficients come from published field trials in Nigeria: the Nigerian Journal of Soil and Environmental Research (2008) on legume nitrogen replacement values; a 1999 study of legume nitrogen contributions at Kaduna and Bauchi; Kureh, Kamara and Tarfa (2006) on Striga reduction from legume rotation; Yusuf and colleagues (2009) in Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment on maize yield after soybean and cowpea; a 2022 Heliyon study on maize yields at Iburu and Zaria; and FAO Irrigation Water Management Training Manual 3 for crop water needs. Default fertilizer and grain prices are editable and based on Nigerian market reports from 2025 and 2026. Software: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Gunicorn, Pydantic, PyYAML, httpx, prometheus client, pystac client, planetary computer, rasterio, numpy, pyproj, MapLibre GL JS (BSD 3 Clause) and OpenStreetMap map tiles (ODbL). Use of AI tools: we used Claude by Anthropic as a coding assistant to draft parts of the code, dashboard, slides and documentation, all reviewed, tested and edited by the team. The season classifier is a transparent rule based model, not a machine learning model. Team: Jothan Jerry Kato (lead), Adamilo Aaron Daniel, Umar Faruq Oladoja, Miracle Mathew, Sadiq Bashir Abdullahi, Ndazibari Charles Joshua.
